cf.title: Fix pg_combinebackup with truncated intermediate incremental backups

input.subject: Re: BUG #19776: pg_combinebackup ignores the truncation_block_length of an intermediate incremental backup

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at levels 1a, 1b or 2. The thread states the problem with a bug report and reproducer (BUG #19776), the reviewer in message #3 confirmed the failure on master and the pass with v2, and the fix adds no user-visible surface. The remaining gaps are about tests and branch choice, which a committer can settle.

brief.title: Fix pg_combinebackup with truncated intermediate incremental backups
brief.problem: pg_combinebackup can restore stale rows when an intermediate incremental backup truncated a relation and a later backup extended it again without writing every block in that range, for example after COPY bulk extension. reconstruct_from_incremental_file() checks only the latest backup's truncation_block_length, so the unwritten blocks are copied from a backup taken before the truncation. Anyone who restores from a chain of incremental backups is affected.
brief.proposed_design: While reconstruct_from_incremental_file() walks backward through the chain, it tracks a running truncation_block_length upper bound and lowers it whenever an incremental backup has a smaller value. Unassigned blocks at or above that bound stay unassigned and are written as zeroes. The bound applies after the current file's own blocks are taken, applies only to incremental files, and also clears full_copy_possible.
author_claims: Without the fix, pg_combinebackup sources unwritten blocks from a pre-truncation backup and brings back stale rows.
Unassigned blocks past the tightened bound are written as zeroes.
v2 is a rebase of v1 with no functional changes.
The extended 011_ib_truncation.pl covers an intermediate truncation followed by COPY bulk extension.
brief.thread_state: One reviewer, Raja Sai Pranav, tested v2 on master (the new test fails without the fix and passes with it), asked for a clearer comment, and gave LGTM on v3 without re-running the TAP suite on v3. Fujii Masao is listed as a CommitFest reviewer but has not posted in the visible thread.
unclear: The new test passes without the fix on a --with-segsize-blocks=6 build, so the test cannot detect the bug in that CI configuration.
No test covers the full_copy_possible = false line; the reviewer could not build that case through the server.
The material does not say which branches need the fix or whether it will be back-patched.
Nobody has re-run the TAP suite on v3; the pass result comes from v2.

questions: Which branches need this fix, and does the patch apply to each of them?
Can the test be made to fail without the fix on a --with-segsize-blocks=6 build, for example with a truncation point inside the re-extended segment?
Can any test, perhaps one that builds backup files by hand, cover the full_copy_possible = false line?
Does the pg_combinebackup TAP suite pass on v3, given that the reported pass result is from v2?
What should users do who already restored from an affected chain and may have stale rows?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows the incremental backup and pg_combinebackup reconstruction code. Fujii Masao is listed as a CommitFest reviewer but has not posted in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the correctness of every backup that pg_combinebackup reconstructs from an incremental chain, on every branch that gets the fix. A mistake in the new bound would write zeroes over valid blocks.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted a rebase in message #2 and a v3 after the review in message #3, which shows active follow-up within the first two weeks.

priority.reason: The bug restores stale rows for users of incremental backup chains, and the fix touches one source file and one test file with no new user-visible surface. A reviewer already confirmed the failure and the fix on master.

provisional_note: The code was not read, so the logic of the running bound and of the full_copy_possible line rests on the reviewer's account in message #3. The segment-boundary case on --with-segsize-blocks builds has no test.

precedents_retrieved.title: teach pg_combinebackup to detect deleted files where possible
precedents_retrieved.summary: pg_combinebackup would look up every file of the final input backup in its backup_manifest and warn about manifest entries that are missing on disk. This catches files deleted from the most recent backup, without reading or checksumming file contents.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas withdrew the patch because no one besides David Steele asked for it. He had mixed feelings about it: the check covers only missing files in the final backup and may give users a false sense of security, and pg_verifybackup already does full verification. Amul Sul reviewed the code but took no position on the idea.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Nobody else has responded. Hence, I'm withdrawing this patch.

precedents_retrieved.title: File level incremental backup
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Robert Haas, Fujii Masao, Bruce Momjian
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add file-level incremental backup to pg_basebackup: given the LSN or directory of a previous backup, send only data files containing blocks with an LSN newer than the threshold, and record a backup_profile file listing every file with its LSN, size and modification time. Reassembling a full backup from a base and an incremental backup was left to a separate restore tool, shown only as a Python prototype, with a C pg_restorebackup planned.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Committers did not accept the design: it reads every file even when nothing has changed and sends whole files when a single block has changed, so it offered little over timestamp-based tools and would leave file-level code to support after a block-level approach existed. Earlier feedback on avoiding the full read and on the backup profile had not been incorporated. The tool needed to reconstruct a usable backup was not part of the patch weeks after the final CommitFest deadline. Robert Haas proposed marking it Rejected, and Michael Paquier agreed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
At least 4 committers have looked at it and none of them are
convinced by the current design; feedback from almost half a year ago
hasn't been incorporated; obviously-needed parts of the patch
(pg_restorebackup) are missing weeks after the last CF deadline.

precedents_retrieved.title: Incremental Materialized View Maintenance
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add incremental materialized views (CREATE INCREMENTAL MATERIALIZED VIEW) that Postgres keeps current in the same transaction as base table changes, using AFTER triggers and transition tables. The patch computes deltas from the view definition and applies them to the view, with support for joins, some built-in aggregates, EXISTS subqueries and outer joins.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier marked the entry Returned with Feedback after a month with no update. In July 2022 huyajun had reported bugs: a deadlock between TRUNCATE and concurrent INSERT, wrong counts after concurrent DELETEs, crashes on mismatched column lists, and an unwanted unique index on cross joins. The author said he was still working on them. Paquier also noted little design discussion in three years, and Greg Stark had earlier called the patch hard to review.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There has been some feedback sent lately and no update
for one month, so I am marking it as RwF for now.

precedents_retrieved.title: Consider incremental sort for fractional paths in generate_orderappend_paths
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch extends get_cheapest_fractional_path_for_pathkeys() so it can optionally add an incremental sort on top of partially sorted child paths when generate_orderedappend_paths() builds fractional paths for LIMIT queries. This is the follow-up to an already committed change that made generate_orderedappend_paths() consider fractional cheapest paths.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The PoC was incomplete: execution failed with a segfault in CheckVarSlotCompatibility, the patch failed tests for months, and building incremental sort paths only to discard most of them looked too expensive. After two months without progress, Andres Freund proposed returned with feedback, and the author agreed it needed much more work than the commitfest allowed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think it's a useful improvement, but it needs much more work
than is doable by the end of this CF.

precedents_retrieved.title: Move backup-related code to xlogbackup.c/.h
precedents_retrieved.summary: Move the backup code, about 700 lines, from xlog.c and xlogfuncs.c into xlogbackup.c/.h to shrink xlog.c and keep backup code in one file. New Get/Set functions on XLogCtl fields let xlogbackup.c use state that stays in xlog.c.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier objected that the new accessor functions make xlogbackup.c call back into xlog.c, which creates a circular dependency between the two files. Alvaro Herrera and Michael Paquier also preferred to keep the SQL functions in xlogfuncs.c. After the thread went quiet in October 2022, the commitfest manager rejected the entry because reviewers were not convinced of the basic approach, and suggested starting with a discussion of the goals.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It looks like neither reviewer has been really convinced this is the
direction they want to go and I think that's why the thread has been
pretty dead since last October.

precedents_retrieved.title: Unified file access using virtual file descriptors
precedents_retrieved.summary: Make virtual file descriptors (VFDs) the common interface for most non-buffer-cache, non-WAL files, adding sequential read/write, seek/tell, append and ferror-style error calls to fd.c. A second patch converts many callers from system or C library file calls to VFDs, as groundwork for transparent encryption, compression or checksums.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch failed to compile on CFbot (an undeclared MAXIMUM_VFD in fd.c), and the author did not post a new version after this was reported. The commitfest manager returned it with feedback for that reason, and no design review appears in the thread.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
With no update to the thread and the compilation still failing I'm
marking this as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Vacuuming relations on full tablespaces (Add EMERGENCY option)
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add an EMERGENCY option to VACUUM so it can run on a full tablespace by not growing the visibility map and free space map, letting it reach the truncation step and free space. The patch did this by adding extended versions of visibilitymap_pin() and RecordPageWithFreeSpace() and by passing the option through vacuumlazy.c.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas objected that changing the calling convention of visibilitymap_pin() and RecordPageWithFreeSpace() was too invasive. He said the revised patch did not address this and that its early return in visibilitymap_set() for an invalid buffer would not be acceptable. The patch then stopped applying to master, and the author sent no update for about three weeks after Haribabu Kommi asked for a rebase, so the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The patch has gotten a lot smaller, and that's clearly good, but
introducing extended versions of those functions still seems like a
thing we should try to avoid.

precedents_retrieved.title: TRUNCATE on foreign tables
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add an optional ExecForeignTruncate callback to FdwRoutine so that TRUNCATE works on foreign tables, including foreign partitions of a partitioned table. The callback gets the foreign tables of one server as a list, with DropBehavior and restart_seqs, and postgres_fdw sends one remote TRUNCATE for them.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier marked it returned with feedback because the implementation, the docs and the tests needed more work. The open issues at that point were ONLY handling, since TRUNCATE ONLY on a local foreign table could truncate the whole inheritance tree on the remote server, and a possible separate truncatable option for postgres_fdw. Missing postgres_fdw documentation and missing inheritance tests were also still open.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: For now, as the patch needs more work for its implementation, docs and tests, I am marking it as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
Reverted commit(s): Ensure that RowExprs and whole-row Vars produce the expected column names.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
In commit bf7ca1587, I had the bright idea that we could make the
result of a whole-row Var (that is, foo.*) track any column aliases
that had been applied to the FROM entry the Var refers to.  However,
that's not terribly logically consistent, because now the output of
the Var is no longer of the named composite type that the Var claims
to emit.  bf7ca1587 tried to handle that by changing the output
tuple values to be labeled with a blessed RECORD type, but that's
really pretty disastrous: we can wind up storing such tuples onto
disk, whereupon they're not readable by other sessions.

The only practical fix I can see is to give up on what bf7ca1587
tried to do, and say that the column names of tuples produced by
a whole-row Var are always those of the underlying named composite
type, query aliases or no.  While this introduces some inconsistencies,
it removes others, so it's not that awful in the abstract.  What *is*
kind of awful is to make such a behavioral change in a back-patched
bug fix.  But corrupt data is worse, so back-patched it will be.

(A workaround available to anyone who's unhappy about this is to
introduce an extra level of sub-SELECT, so that the whole-row Var is
referring to the sub-SELECT's output and not to a named table type.
Then the Var is of type RECORD to begin with and there's no issue.)

Per report from Miles Delahunty.  The faulty commit dates to 9.5,
so back-patch to all supported branches.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Reject concurrent sequence refreshes".
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Reject concurrent sequence refreshes".
Reverted commit(s): Reject concurrent sequence refreshes.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit f38afa4abb04e85530c94b88daf11c089375daca.

That commit fixed a race that could leave stale sequence values on the
subscriber after 'ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... REFRESH SEQUENCES'. It did so by
raising an ERROR during 'ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... REFRESH SEQUENCES'
whenever a sequence synchronization worker was already running for the
subscription.

That approach caused intermittent buildfarm failures, because the existing
tests did not ensure the sequencesync worker had stopped before executing
'ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... REFRESH SEQUENCES'. While discussing how to fix
the tests, we concluded that blocking the command while a sequencesync
worker is running is inconvenient for users. So we will fix the original
race differently in a follow-up commit.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found: the corpus search returned no earlier proposal for the same or a similar idea, and the thread does not point to an earlier discussion. This is a bug fix for data restored from an incremental backup chain, so no prior rejection reason applies from this angle.

From the standards and compatibility angle, this bug fix in reconstruct_from_incremental_file() gives no grounds for rejection. It adds no syntax, keyword, GUC, catalog object, psql behaviour or dump format. It uses the existing truncation_block_length field in incremental files, so backups taken before the fix stay valid input. The only behaviour change is that pg_combinebackup no longer restores truncated, stale blocks and writes zeroes instead, which is the intended correct result. The material does not yet say which branches get the fix, but a committer can settle that at commit time.

No objection from the replication and on-disk angle. The patch changes how pg_combinebackup picks the source backup for each block. It does not change the incremental file format, WAL, the catalog, the wire protocol or any extension API, so it adds no pg_upgrade or rolling-upgrade concern. The design writes zeroes for blocks at or above the lowest truncation_block_length seen in the chain, unless a later backup supplied them. This keeps the existing invariant that a combined backup matches the latest backup state, and the reviewer in message #3 checked that reasoning. Several points could not be checked without the code. The segment-boundary case on --with-segsize-blocks builds has no test, and neither does the full_copy_possible line. The material also does not say which branches get the fix. Users who already restored from an affected chain have no way to detect stale rows, but that is a reason to fix the bug, not an objection to this design.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect. It changes how pg_combinebackup, a client tool run by the backup operator on files that operator already owns, picks block sources, and it adds no SQL surface, privilege, role or setting. Resurrected rows are a data correctness problem, and the fix narrows what gets restored, so it gives no new access.

This is a contained correctness fix inside pg_combinebackup that adds no API, GUC or catalog state and costs nothing for non-users, so there is no maintenance or fit objection. The remaining gaps are level 4 or committability items: the new test does not detect the bug on a --with-segsize-blocks=6 build, the full_copy_possible line has no test, v3 has not been re-run, and Fujii Masao has not posted.

This is a correctness fix inside pg_combinebackup's reconstruction logic. No existing feature, option or external tool gives a correct combined backup when an intermediate incremental backup truncated a relation, so the already-exists angle has nothing to raise.

This is a data-correctness bug fix for pg_combinebackup, reported by a user as BUG #19776 with a reproducer. Anyone restoring from an incremental chain can get stale rows back, so demand is real, and only the restore path pays the cost.
